days.title: Las cinco vocales
days.objective: Recognize and pronounce the five Spanish vowel sounds and read simple words aloud by syllable.
days.paretoFocus: Spanish spelling is fully phonetic, so mastering the five vowel sounds now makes every word you meet from here on readable on sight.
drills: Say the five Spanish vowels aloud in order: a, e, i, o, u.
Read three short words aloud, syllable by syllable.
Write down two Spanish words you can now sound out.

items: Name the five Spanish vowels.
Explain why Spanish vowels never change sound.
Divide a short word into syllables.

activities.title: Las vocales
activities.intro: Spanish has five pure vowel sounds, one per letter, that never reduce or change the way English vowels do. Words divide cleanly into syllables around those vowels, which is the first skill for reading Spanish aloud.

items.note: Each letter always makes the same sound.
ca-sa: two syllables, each with one vowel.
me-sa: two syllables.
a-mi-go: three syllables.
u-no: two syllables.

activities.title: Sonidos y sílabas
activities.intro: Practice hearing the five vowel sounds and dividing short words into syllables.

questions.prompt: Which word has three syllables?
questions.explanation: amigo divides as a-mi-go, three syllables; casa and mesa each have two, uno has two.

questions.prompt: Which vowel appears twice in 'casa'?
questions.explanation: casa is spelled c-a-s-a; the vowel a appears in both syllables.

questions.prompt: Complete the missing vowel: c_sa. (house)
questions.explanation: casa is spelled with two a's, c-a-s-a.

questions.prompt: Complete the missing vowel: _no. (one)
questions.explanation: uno starts with u.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish word for: 'friend', from its syllables.
questions.explanation: amigo divides as a-mi-go.

activities.title: Practicamos las vocales
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners quiz each other on simple words built from the five vowel sounds.

days.title: La ñ, la ll, la rr y la h muda
days.objective: Distinguish and pronounce the Spanish letters ñ, ll and rr, and recognize that h is always silent.
days.paretoFocus: These spelling points cause the most common beginner mispronunciations and, in the case of ñ, can change a word's meaning entirely.
drills: Say año and ano aloud and notice the different sound.
Read perro and pero aloud, holding the rr longer.
Read hola aloud without pronouncing the h.

items: Explain the sound difference between ñ and plain n.
Say perro and pero and identify which one is trilled.
Explain what the silent h does to the word hola.

activities.title: Ñ, LL, RR y la H
activities.intro: The letter ñ is a separate letter with its own nasal sound, not just n with a mark. The double ll sounds like the y in yes, as in calle (street). A double rr is a strong trilled sound, different from a single r between vowels. The letter h is always silent in Spanish, no matter where it appears.

items.note: ñ sounds like the 'ny' in canyon.
without the ñ this is a different, crude word; never confuse them.
double r is a strong trill.
a single r between vowels is soft, not trilled.
the h is silent, so hola is pronounced exactly like ola (wave).

activities.title: Escucha y distingue
activities.intro: Practice telling apart ñ, ll, rr and the silent h.

questions.prompt: Which word means 'dog'?
questions.explanation: perro, with the trilled rr, means dog; pero, with a single soft r, means but.

questions.prompt: Which word is spelled with ñ, not a plain n?
questions.explanation: año uses the separate letter ñ, pronounced like the 'ny' in canyon.

questions.prompt: Complete the word for 'street', spelled with double l: ca___.
questions.explanation: calle is spelled with ll.

questions.prompt: Complete the letter needed to spell 'year' correctly: a_o.
questions.explanation: año needs ñ; without it, the word means something completely different.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish word for: 'hospital', which begins with a silent letter.
questions.explanation: hospital begins with a silent h, so it is pronounced as if it started with the o.

activities.title: Sonidos casi iguales
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners test each other on words that sound almost the same.

days.title: C, Z, S: la distinción castellana; G y J
days.objective: Pronounce c (before e/i) and z with the Castilian sound distinct from s, and tell apart the two sounds of g and the sound of j.
days.paretoFocus: Getting the distinción right from the start avoids relearning later, since it is the sound model this course teaches, even though much of the Spanish-speaking world merges these sounds.
drills: Say cielo, zapato and casa aloud, noticing the different first sound in cielo and zapato versus casa.
Read gente and jugar aloud, comparing the two similar-sounding consonants.
Read guitarra aloud, noticing gu keeps the hard g sound.

items: Explain the Castilian distinción between c/z and s.
Say which letter, g or j, makes the same sound before e and i.
Explain why guitarra keeps a hard g sound before i.

activities.title: Distinción: C, Z, S / G, J
activities.intro: In central and northern Spain, c before e or i and z are pronounced with the tongue between the teeth, different from s; that is the model this course teaches, though many regions and all of America merge them (seseo), which is not an error, simply a different model. g before e or i and j share one sound; gu before e or i keeps the hard g.

items.note: c before i is pronounced like the th in this model.
z is always pronounced with that same sound.
s is a plain s sound, different from z and from c before e/i.
g before e sounds like Spanish j.
j always has this same throaty sound.

activities.title: C, Z, S, G, J
activities.intro: Practice telling apart the c/z sound from s, and g from j.

questions.prompt: Which word starts with the same sound as 'zapato'?
questions.explanation: cielo starts with c before i, pronounced like z in this model; casa's s is a different sound.

questions.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the j in 'jugar'?
questions.explanation: g before e sounds identical to j.

questions.prompt: Complete the missing letter: _apato. (shoe)
questions.explanation: zapato starts with z.

questions.prompt: Complete the missing letter that keeps the hard g sound: g_itarra. (guitar)
questions.explanation: guitarra inserts a silent u to keep the hard g sound before the following i.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'shoe', from its syllables.
questions.explanation: zapato begins with z, which in the Castilian model is the th of think, not an s.

activities.title: Sonidos parecidos
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners test each other on words with the c/z/s and g/j sounds.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Cielo, con el sonido de la zeta.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Casa, con el sonido de la ese.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Gente, con el sonido de la jota.

days.title: El acento de intensidad: agudas, llanas y esdrújulas
days.objective: Identify where the spoken stress falls in a Spanish word and know when that stress must be written as an accent mark.
days.paretoFocus: The three stress rules predict the written accent on almost every Spanish word, so learning them now makes spelling automatic instead of memorized word by word.
drills: Say esta and está aloud, stressing a different syllable each time.
Say papa and papá aloud and notice the meaning changes.
Say hablo and habló aloud and notice the written accent.

items: State the rule for words ending in a vowel, n or s.
State the rule for words that break that pattern.
Explain what an esdrújula word is and give its rule.

activities.title: Agudas, llanas y esdrújulas
activities.intro: Spanish words are stressed on a predictable syllable. Words stressed on the last syllable that end in a vowel, n or s need a written accent; words stressed on the second-to-last syllable that end in anything else need one; words stressed on the third-to-last syllable always need one.

items.note: stress falls naturally on the first syllable; no accent needed.
stress falls on the last syllable and the word ends in a vowel, so it needs a written accent.

items.en: pope (el Papa); in much of America, potato (in Spain: patata)
items.note: stressed naturally on the first syllable; no accent.
stressed on the last syllable ending in a vowel, so it takes an accent.
stressed naturally on the first syllable, no accent.

activities.title: ¿Dónde está el acento?
activities.intro: Practice deciding when a word needs a written accent.

questions.prompt: Which of these words needs a written accent?
questions.explanation: habló is stressed on the last syllable and ends in a vowel, so it needs a written accent; the others are stressed naturally.

questions.prompt: Which word means 'dad', stressed on the last syllable?
questions.explanation: papá is stressed on the final syllable ending in a vowel, so it needs the accent that distinguishes it from papa.

questions.prompt: Add the accent mark if needed: pap___. (dad)
questions.explanation: papá is stressed on the last syllable ending in a vowel, so the tilde is required.

questions.prompt: Add the accent mark if needed: est___. (is / is located)
questions.explanation: está is stressed on the last syllable and ends in a vowel, so the accent is required.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'heart', stressed on the last syllable.
questions.explanation: corazón is stressed on the final syllable and ends in n, so it breaks the default rule and must write the accent.

activities.title: Con o sin tilde
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners test each other on word pairs that differ only by a written accent.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Papá, with an accent, is different.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Habló, con tilde, es otra palabra.
lines.en: Habló, with an accent, is another word.

days.title: La tilde diacrítica, y los signos ¿ ¡
days.objective: Tell apart the small set of Spanish word pairs that differ only by a written accent, and always open questions and exclamations with the inverted marks.
days.paretoFocus: These short high-frequency words appear in almost every sentence, so confusing sí/si or tú/tu changes meaning even though the spelling looks nearly identical.
drills: Say si and sí aloud and explain the difference in meaning.
Say tu and tú aloud and explain the difference.
Write a short question and a short exclamation with the correct opening marks.

items: Explain what a tilde diacrítica does.
Give the meaning difference between si and sí.
State the rule for opening question and exclamation marks in Spanish.

activities.title: Tilde diacrítica: sí, tú, qué
activities.intro: A small group of short words are spelled identically except for a written accent that has nothing to do with the stress rules; the accent simply distinguishes two different words. Spanish also opens every question with ¿ and every exclamation with ¡, not only at the end.

items.note: no accent; the conditional word.
with an accent; the answer word.
no accent; the possessive.
with an accent; the pronoun.
questions open with an inverted question mark; qué with an accent asks a question.

activities.title: Sí o si, tú o tu
activities.intro: Practice the accent that separates these short word pairs.

questions.prompt: Which word means 'yes'?
questions.explanation: sí with the accent means yes; si without it means if.

questions.prompt: Which word is the subject pronoun 'you', not the possessive?
questions.explanation: tú with the accent is the subject pronoun; tu without it is the possessive, as in tu casa.

questions.prompt: Add the accent if needed: s___. (yes, the answer word)
questions.explanation: sí needs the accent to distinguish it from si (if).

questions.prompt: Add the accent if needed: t___. (you, the pronoun)
questions.explanation: tú needs the accent to distinguish it from tu (your).

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'What?', with the correct opening punctuation.
questions.explanation: Spanish opens a question with an inverted question mark and closes it with the standard one.

activities.title: Con o sin tilde diacrítica
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners test each other on the small word pairs that only an accent tells apart.

days.title: Hola, buenos días, adiós
days.objective: Greet someone appropriately for the time of day and say goodbye using common fixed expressions.
days.paretoFocus: Greetings are the very first exchange in every real interaction, so having them automatic removes the first friction point of speaking.
drills: Practice saying hello and goodbye at three different times of day.
Say ¿qué tal? and give a short reply.
Write out a short greeting exchange for the morning.

items: Give the greeting used only until noon.
Give two ways to say goodbye.
Explain what ¿qué tal? asks.

activities.title: Saludos y despedidas
activities.intro: Spanish greetings change with the time of day: buenos días until midday, buenas tardes in the afternoon, buenas noches at night. ¿Qué tal? is a casual way to ask how someone is, and hasta luego is a common informal goodbye.

items.note: Used at any time of day.
Used until around midday.
Used from midday until nightfall.
Used at night, for greeting or leaving.
A casual way to ask how someone is.

activities.title: Saludos
activities.intro: Practice choosing the right greeting for the moment.

questions.prompt: Which greeting do you use in the morning?
questions.explanation: Buenos días is used until around midday.

questions.prompt: How many syllables does 'buenas' have?
questions.explanation: buenas divides as bue-nas, two syllables, using the same syllable-counting skill from your very first lesson.

questions.prompt: Complete the night greeting: Buenas ___.
questions.explanation: Buenas noches greets or bids farewell at night.

questions.prompt: Complete the casual way to ask how someone is: ¿Qué ___?
questions.explanation: ¿Qué tal? is the casual way to ask how someone is doing.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'Hello, good afternoon.'
questions.explanation: Buenas tardes is used from midday until nightfall, and hola works at any hour.

activities.title: Buenos días
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people greet each other, ask how it's going, and say goodbye.

days.title: Me llamo... ¿Cómo te llamas?
days.objective: Ask someone's name, give your own, and spell it aloud using the Spanish alphabet.
days.paretoFocus: Exchanging names is the second thing that happens in almost every real conversation, right after the greeting, and spelling your name aloud is a skill you will use constantly in Spain.
drills: Say your name using me llamo.
Ask a partner ¿cómo te llamas? and answer their reply.
Spell your own name aloud using the Spanish letter names.

items: Give the phrase for telling someone your name.
Give the question for asking someone's name.
Name three letters of the Spanish alphabet that sound different from English.

activities.title: Me llamo / ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.intro: Me llamo literally means 'I call myself' and is the ordinary way to give your name; the question form is ¿cómo te llamas?, and ¿y tú? throws the question back. Spelling a name uses the Spanish letter names, and several sound different from English.

items.note: Literally 'I call myself Ana'.
The standard informal way to ask a name.
Throws the question back.
The first five Spanish letter names, used to spell a name aloud.
h is 'hache', i is just 'i', j is 'jota'.

activities.title: Nombres y letras
activities.intro: Practice giving and asking for a name, and spelling it aloud.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to ask someone's name?
questions.explanation: ¿Cómo te llamas? literally asks what you call yourself.

questions.prompt: Which Spanish letter is never pronounced?
questions.explanation: The letter h is always silent in Spanish, as in hola, learned earlier.

questions.prompt: Complete: Me ___ Carlos. (my name is)
questions.explanation: me llamo + name is how you give your own name.

questions.prompt: Complete the question: ¿Cómo te ___? (what's your name)
questions.explanation: llamas is the tú form used in this fixed question.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'My name is Ana.'
questions.explanation: me llamo comes first, then the name.

activities.title: ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two strangers introduce themselves and spell their names.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: My name is Marta. And you?

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Marta: eme, a, erre, te, a.
lines.en: Marta: m, a, r, t, a.

days.title: El verbo ser: identidad, origen y profesión
days.objective: Conjugate and use ser in the present to state who you are, where you are from and what you do.
days.paretoFocus: Ser is one of only four irregular verbs at this level and carries the single most common function in beginner speech: saying who and what you are.
drills: Say soy plus your nationality.
Say a sentence with es de plus a city.
Conjugate ser for yo, tú and él/ella/usted aloud.

items: Give the six forms of ser in the present.
Say a sentence using soy for a profession.
Say a sentence using es de for origin.

activities.title: Ser: soy, eres, es...
activities.intro: Ser is one of the four verbs with its own irregular pattern at this level, and it is used for identity, origin (with de) and profession: statements of what or who someone is.

items.note: soy is the yo form of ser.
eres is the tú form.
es is the él/ella/usted form; de marks origin.
somos is the nosotros form.
sois is the vosotros form, used in Spain for an informal plural you.

activities.title: Formas de ser
activities.intro: Practice the six present-tense forms of ser.

questions.prompt: Which form of ser goes with 'yo'?
questions.explanation: soy is the yo form of ser.

questions.prompt: Which form completes: Ellos ___ de Bilbao.
questions.explanation: son is the ellos/ellas/ustedes form of ser.

questions.prompt: Complete: Yo ___ estudiante. (am)
questions.explanation: soy is used with yo.

questions.prompt: Complete the city name, which starts with the same sound as 'zapato': Somos de ___aragoza.
questions.explanation: Zaragoza starts with the z sound taught alongside zapato a few lessons ago.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'She is from Madrid.'
questions.explanation: es + de + place states origin.

activities.title: Identidad y origen
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people meet and state their nationality, origin and occupation with ser.

lines.en: Hi! I'm Diego. I'm Spanish, from Madrid.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Yes, I'm a student. And you?

days.title: El género de los sustantivos: -o y -a
days.objective: Predict the gender of most Spanish nouns from their -o or -a ending and pair them with el or la.
days.paretoFocus: Getting the article right on sight, using the -o/-a pattern, is what lets every noun you learn from here on slot correctly into a sentence without hesitation.
drills: Sort five nouns into el and la by their ending.
Say el día and la mano aloud and note they break the pattern.
Write three -o nouns and three -a nouns with their article.

items: State the reliable pattern for -o and -a nouns.
Give two nouns that break the pattern.
Explain why el día uses el despite ending in -a.

activities.title: El y la: -o, -a
activities.intro: Most Spanish nouns ending in -o are masculine (el) and most ending in -a are feminine (la); the pattern is reliable but not universal, and a handful of common exceptions must simply be memorized.

items.note: -o ending, masculine, follows the pattern.
-a ending, feminine, follows the pattern.
ends in -a but is masculine, a common exception.
ends in -o but is feminine, a common exception.
ends in -a but is masculine, another memorised exception.

activities.title: El o la
activities.intro: Practice matching el or la to -o and -a nouns, including the exceptions.

questions.prompt: Which article goes with 'problema'?
questions.explanation: el problema is a masculine exception ending in -a.

questions.prompt: Which word follows the regular -a, feminine pattern?
questions.explanation: casa ends in -a and is feminine, the regular pattern; día, mano and mapa are all exceptions.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct article: ___ libro. (the)
questions.explanation: libro ends in -o, so it takes el.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct article, keeping the accent mark on the noun: ___ papá. (the dad)
questions.explanation: papá is masculine regardless of its ending, and keeps its written accent from the stress rules taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'It is the hand.'
questions.explanation: mano is a feminine exception to the -o pattern, so it takes la.

lines.speaker: Me

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: La mano. Termina en o, pero es femenino.

days.title: Sustantivos que no terminan en -o ni en -a
days.objective: Assign the correct gender to nouns that end in a consonant, using the -ción/-dad/-tad pattern for feminine and learning the rest case by case.
days.paretoFocus: A large share of everyday nouns, especially abstract ones ending in -ción or -dad, fall outside the -o/-a pattern, so this second rule covers most of what the first one misses.
drills: Sort estación, ciudad and árbol by gender.
Say three nouns ending in -ción and give their article.
Write one masculine and one feminine consonant-ending noun, with its article.

items: State the rule for nouns ending in -ción, -dad or -tad.
Give the article for árbol and for catedral.
Explain why gender for consonant-ending nouns must often be memorized.

activities.title: Género: consonantes finales
activities.intro: Nouns ending in a consonant do not follow the -o/-a rule; however nouns ending in -ción, -dad or -tad are reliably feminine, while other consonant endings must be learned noun by noun.

items.note: -ción is always feminine.
-dad is always feminine.
-tad is always feminine.
masculine, no rule, simply learned.
feminine, no rule, simply learned.

activities.title: Consonante final
activities.intro: Choose la or el for words like estación, árbol and catedral.

questions.prompt: Which article always goes with words ending in -ción?
questions.explanation: -ción nouns are always feminine, so they take la.

questions.prompt: Which of these words is masculine?
questions.explanation: árbol is masculine, an ending with no reliable clue, simply memorized.

questions.prompt: Complete: ___ libertad es importante. (freedom, the)
questions.explanation: -tad nouns are always feminine.

questions.prompt: Complete with the accented word for 'yes': ___ es la ciudad, no la estación.
questions.explanation: sí with the accent means yes, distinguishing it from si (if), taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'It is the tree.'
questions.explanation: árbol is a masculine consonant-ending noun with no predictable clue, so its article has to be learned with it.

lines.en: The tree. It's masculine, no rule.

lines.speaker: Me

lines.en: The cathedral. It's feminine, no rule.

days.title: El plural: -s, -es, y los, las
days.objective: Form the plural of Spanish nouns with -s or -es and pair them with los or las.
days.paretoFocus: Plural nouns and their articles appear constantly once you start counting, describing groups or talking about more than one thing.
drills: Make libro, ciudad and lápiz plural.
Say los libros and las ciudades aloud.
Write the plural of one noun ending in a vowel and one ending in a consonant.

items: State the plural rule for nouns ending in a vowel.
State the plural rule for nouns ending in a consonant.
Explain the spelling shift in lápiz to lápices.

activities.title: Plurales: -s, -es
activities.intro: Nouns ending in a vowel simply add -s; nouns ending in a consonant add -es; nouns ending in -z change the z to c before adding -es. The plural articles are los (masculine) and las (feminine).

items.note: vowel ending, add -s.
consonant ending, add -es.
z changes to c before -es.
vowel ending, add -s.
consonant ending, add -es.

activities.title: Singular y plural
activities.intro: Practice forming plurals and matching them to los or las.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct plural of 'lápiz'?
questions.explanation: Before -es, z changes to c: lápiz becomes lápices.

questions.prompt: Which plural article goes with 'catedrales'?
questions.explanation: catedral is feminine, so its plural article is las.

questions.prompt: Complete the plural: ciudad___. (cities)
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in a consonant add -es: ciudad becomes ciudades.

questions.prompt: Complete the night farewell: Buenas ___.
questions.explanation: Buenas noches is used at night, learned in your first week.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'the trees and the houses'.
questions.explanation: árbol adds -es and keeps its masculine article; casa adds -s and keeps its feminine one.

activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two learners quiz each other on singular and plural nouns.

lines.hr: Lápices, en plural. La zeta cambia a ce.
lines.en: Pencils, in the plural. The z changes to c.

days.title: Los adjetivos: concordancia de género
days.objective: Match a descriptive adjective's gender to the noun it describes, including adjectives that never change.
days.paretoFocus: Every adjective you use has to agree with its noun, so this pattern applies to nearly every descriptive sentence you will build from here on.
drills: Say a noun phrase with an -o/-a adjective for a masculine and a feminine noun.
Say a sentence with an adjective that does not change, like grande.
Write one masculine and one feminine adjective pair.

items: State the rule for -o/-a adjectives.
Name two adjectives that never change with gender.
Give the feminine form of alto.

activities.title: Adjetivos: -o, -a
activities.intro: Adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine nouns, matching gender the same way nouns do; adjectives ending in other letters, like grande, interesante and azul, stay the same for both genders.

items.note: alto, masculine form.
alta, feminine form.
interesante does not change.
grande does not change.
azul does not change.

activities.title: Concordancia de género
activities.intro: Practice matching adjective gender to the noun, and spotting the ones that never change.

questions.prompt: Which is the feminine form of 'alto'?
questions.explanation: -o adjectives change to -a for feminine nouns.

questions.prompt: Which adjective does not change with gender?
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -e stay the same for masculine and feminine.

questions.explanation: alta is the feminine form of alto.

questions.prompt: Complete the fixed phrase for giving your name: Me ___ Diego.
questions.explanation: me llamo + name is the fixed formula from your earliest lessons.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'the interesting book'.
questions.explanation: Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun, and interesante does not change for gender.

days.title: Los adjetivos: plural y posición
days.objective: Make adjectives agree in number with their noun and place them correctly, including the shortened forms buen and gran before a masculine singular noun.
days.paretoFocus: Number agreement and word order finish the adjective system you started two lessons ago, so descriptions finally come out sounding natural rather than just grammatically present.
drills: Make altos and interesantes plural.
Say un buen amigo and una gran ciudad aloud.
Write a short noun phrase with a plural adjective.

items: State the plural rule for adjectives.
Recall the short form bueno takes right in front of amigo.
State where a descriptive adjective normally goes.

activities.title: Adjetivos: plural, buen, gran
activities.intro: Adjectives take -s or -es to match a plural noun, exactly like nouns do; descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun, but bueno and grande shorten to buen and gran when they come right before a singular noun (bueno only before a masculine one).

items.note: plural adjective matches plural noun.
grande adds -s for the plural.
interesante adds -s for the plural.
bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun.
grande shortens to gran before any singular noun, masculine or feminine.

activities.title: Plural y posición
activities.intro: Pick between buen/bueno and gran/grande, and pluralize adjectives to match the noun.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct plural of 'interesante'?
questions.explanation: -e adjectives add -s for the plural, regardless of gender.

questions.prompt: Which form of 'bueno' is used right before a masculine singular noun?
questions.explanation: bueno shortens to buen right before a masculine singular noun.

questions.prompt: Complete: los chicos alt___. (tall, plural)
questions.explanation: Plural adjectives ending in -o take -os to match a plural masculine noun.

questions.prompt: Complete: Ellos ___ altos. (are)
questions.explanation: son is the ellos/ellas/ustedes form of ser, needed to link the subject to the adjective.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'the big cities'.
questions.explanation: grande adds -s for the plural and follows the noun as usual.

activities.title: Un buen amigo, una gran ciudad
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two friends describe a trip, choosing buen or gran before each noun.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Sí, y las chicas son altas.
lines.en: Yes, and the girls are tall.

days.title: Tú o usted: el registro; vosotros y ustedes
days.objective: Choose between tú and usted according to formality, and between vosotros and ustedes for addressing more than one person in the peninsular system.
days.paretoFocus: Spain distinguishes four ways of saying 'you', and picking the wrong one either sounds needlessly formal with a friend or rude with a stranger, so this choice underlies almost every sentence you will say to someone.
drills: Decide whether tú or usted fits: a shop assistant, a classmate.
Say the plural informal and plural formal you for a group of friends and a group of strangers.
Explain the difference between the Spain system and the Latin American system.

items: Give the four ways of saying you in peninsular Spanish.
State which one is used for a stranger.
State which one all of Latin America uses for every plural.

activities.title: Tú, usted, vosotros, ustedes
activities.intro: Spain distinguishes four second persons: tú (informal singular), usted (formal singular), vosotros/vosotras (informal plural) and ustedes (formal plural). This course teaches that peninsular four-way system, though all of Latin America uses ustedes for every plural, informal or formal, without that being wrong.

items.note: used with friends, family, children.
used with strangers, in shops, with elders you don't know.
used in Spain for a group of friends or family.
used in Spain for a group you address formally; in Latin America, used for every plural.
usted takes the same verb form as él/ella.

activities.title: Tú, usted, vosotros, ustedes
activities.intro: Practice choosing the right form of you for the person or group you're addressing.

questions.prompt: Which form would you use with a group of friends, in Spain?
questions.explanation: vosotros is the informal plural used in Spain for a group of friends or family.

questions.prompt: Which form does all of Latin America use for every plural, formal or informal?
questions.explanation: Latin American Spanish uses ustedes for every plural, with no separate informal plural.

questions.prompt: Complete: to speak with a stranger in a shop, you use ___.
questions.explanation: usted is the formal singular, used with strangers.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct article: ___ mano. (the hand)
questions.explanation: mano is a feminine exception to the -o pattern, taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'Are you (formal) from Madrid?'
questions.explanation: usted takes the same verb form as él/ella.

activities.title: ¿Tú o usted?
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people run through when to use each of the four peninsular forms of you.

lines.speaker: Partner
lines.en: With a friend, you use tú.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Sí, y con un grupo de amigos, vosotros.
lines.en: Yes, and with a group of friends, vosotros.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Y con un grupo formal, ustedes.
lines.en: And with a formal group, ustedes.

days.title: Los pronombres personales, y cuándo aparecen
days.objective: List the full set of Spanish subject pronouns and use them only when needed for contrast, since the verb ending already shows who is doing the action.
days.paretoFocus: Spanish drops the subject pronoun in almost every sentence, so knowing when to include it, for contrast or clarity, is what keeps your speech from sounding like a word-for-word English translation.
drills: List all six Spanish subject pronouns.
Say a sentence with no subject pronoun, relying on the verb ending.
Say a sentence with a pronoun included, for contrast.

items: List the six subject pronouns.
Explain why Spanish usually omits them.
Give an example where including the pronoun adds contrast.

activities.title: Pronombres personales
activities.intro: The Spanish subject pronouns are yo, tú, él/ella/usted, nosotros/nosotras, vosotros/vosotras, ellos/ellas/ustedes. Because the verb ending already signals who the subject is, Spanish usually drops the pronoun and only includes it for emphasis or contrast.

items.note: yo is normally dropped; soy already shows it is 'I'.
nosotros/nosotras for a group including the speaker.
ellos/ellas for a group not including the speaker or listener.

items.hr: Yo soy alto, ella es baja.
items.en: I am tall, she is short.
items.note: here yo and ella are kept, for contrast.
tú is often kept in questions for clarity, though it isn't required.

activities.title: Pronombres
activities.intro: Practice the subject pronouns and when to keep or drop them.

questions.prompt: Which pronoun refers to a group that includes the speaker?
questions.explanation: nosotros/nosotras includes the speaker.

questions.prompt: Why does Spanish usually drop the subject pronoun?
options: Because the verb ending already shows it.
Because it's only used in questions.
questions.answer: Because the verb ending already shows it.
questions.explanation: The verb ending already signals the subject, so the pronoun is often unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Complete with the pronoun for a group that excludes both speaker and listener: ___ son de Bilbao. (they)
questions.explanation: ellos/ellas refers to a group excluding both speaker and listener.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct article: ___ ciudad es grande. (the)
questions.explanation: ciudad ends in -dad, always feminine, so it takes la.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'I am tall, she is short.'
questions.explanation: Both pronouns are kept here to contrast the two people.

activities.title: Yo, tú, nosotros, ellos
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people talk about themselves and others, keeping pronouns only where they add contrast.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Yes, I'm from Madrid. And you?

lines.speaker: Me
lines.hr: Yo soy alto, y tú eres baja.
lines.en: I am tall, and you are short.

days.title: Verbos regulares en -ar
days.objective: Conjugate and use regular -ar verbs in the present tense for everyday actions.
days.paretoFocus: Regular -ar verbs are the largest verb group in Spanish, so this single pattern unlocks hundreds of everyday actions at once.
drills: Conjugate hablar for all six persons.
Say a sentence with trabajar and one with estudiar.
Write two sentences using -ar verbs about your own routine.

items: Give the six present-tense endings for -ar verbs.
Say the yo form of trabajar.
Say the nosotros form of cantar.

activities.title: Presente: -ar
activities.intro: Regular -ar verbs share one set of endings in the present: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. hablar, trabajar, estudiar, escuchar and cantar all follow this pattern exactly.

items.note: hablar, yo form: -o.
trabajar, tú form: -as.
estudiar, nosotros form: -amos.
escuchar, vosotros form: -áis.
cantar, ellos form: -an.

activities.title: Verbos en -ar
activities.intro: Fill in the missing -ar ending for hablar, trabajar and estudiar.

questions.prompt: What is the yo ending for -ar verbs?
questions.explanation: The yo form of -ar verbs always ends in -o: hablo, trabajo, estudio.

questions.prompt: Which form corresponds to 'nosotros' for trabajar?
questions.explanation: The nosotros ending for -ar verbs is -amos.

questions.prompt: Complete: Ella ___ español. (speaks)
questions.explanation: The él/ella/usted ending for -ar verbs is -a.

questions.prompt: Complete: Vosotros ___ música. (listen to)
questions.explanation: The vosotros ending for -ar verbs is -áis.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'the interesting cities'.
questions.explanation: ciudad takes -es and interesante takes -s in the plural, both patterns from earlier lessons.

activities.title: Hablar, trabajar, estudiar
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people talk about what they speak, where they work and study, using regular -ar verbs.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Yes, I speak Spanish and Portuguese.

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Yes, I work in Madrid. And you?

lines.speaker: Me
lines.en: Do you all study a lot?

days.title: Verbos regulares en -er e -ir
days.objective: Conjugate and use regular -er and -ir verbs in the present tense.
days.paretoFocus: Together with -ar, these two patterns cover the present tense of almost every regular verb you will meet, completing the core engine of everyday Spanish.
drills: Conjugate comer and vivir for all six persons.
Say a sentence with leer and one with escribir.
Write two sentences, one -er verb and one -ir verb, about daily life.

items: Give the six present-tense endings for -er verbs.
Give the six present-tense endings for -ir verbs.
Say where -er and -ir verbs differ in their endings.

activities.title: Presente: -er, -ir
activities.intro: -er verbs take -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en; -ir verbs take the same endings except for nosotros and vosotros, -imos and -ís. comer, beber and leer follow the -er pattern; vivir, escribir and abrir follow the -ir pattern.

items.note: comer, yo form: -o.
beber, tú form: -es.
vivir, él/ella form: -e, same as -er.
escribir, nosotros form: -imos, different from -er's -emos.
leer, vosotros form: -éis.

activities.title: Verbos en -er, -ir
activities.intro: Match each subject to the right -er or -ir ending for comer and vivir.

questions.prompt: What is the nosotros ending for -ir verbs?
questions.explanation: -ir verbs use -imos for nosotros, unlike -er verbs, which use -emos.

questions.prompt: Which form corresponds to 'él' for vivir?
questions.explanation: The él/ella/usted ending for -ir verbs is -e, the same as for -er verbs.

questions.prompt: Complete: Yo ___ en casa. (eat)
questions.explanation: The yo ending for -er verbs is -o.

questions.prompt: Complete: Ellos ___ cartas. (write)
questions.explanation: The ellos/ellas/ustedes ending for -ir verbs is -en, the same as for -er verbs.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'The tall boy drinks water.'
questions.explanation: alto agrees with the masculine chico, an agreement pattern from several lessons earlier.

activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two roommates compare routines, conjugating comer, beber and vivir as they talk.

lines.en: Yes, I eat at home. Do you drink coffee?

days.title: Estar: ¿dónde están las cosas y las personas?
days.objective: Conjugate estar in the present and use it with aquí, allí and en to say where something or someone is.
days.paretoFocus: Location is one of the most immediately useful things you can say or ask, whether it's about a place, an object or a person.
drills: Conjugate estar for all six persons.
Say a sentence with aquí and one with allí.
Ask where something is using estar.

items: Give the six forms of estar in the present.
Give the difference between aquí and allí.
Say a sentence using estar + en + a place.

activities.title: Estar: estoy, estás, está...
activities.intro: Estar is the second of the four irregular verbs at this level and is used for location, where something or someone physically is. Aquí means here, allí means there, and en marks a place.

items.note: estoy is the yo form of estar.
estás is the tú form; dónde asks for a place.
está is the él/ella/usted form.
estamos is the nosotros form; allí means over there.
están is the ellos/ellas/ustedes form.

activities.title: Estar y el lugar
activities.intro: Practice conjugating estar and using it to say where something is.

questions.prompt: Which form of estar corresponds to 'nosotros'?
questions.explanation: estamos is the nosotros form of estar.

questions.prompt: Which word asks specifically about a place?
questions.explanation: dónde asks specifically about location.

questions.prompt: Complete: Yo ___ aquí. (am)
questions.explanation: estoy is the yo form of estar.

questions.prompt: Complete the plural of 'interesante': los libros interesant___.
questions.explanation: interesante adds -s in the plural, a pattern from a few lessons earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'They are at the station.'
questions.explanation: están is the ellos/ellas/ustedes form of estar, followed by en + the place.

activities.title: ¿Dónde estás?
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people ask and say where they and others are.

lines.speaker: Partner
lines.en: And the books? Where are they?

days.title: Estar: cómo te sientes y cómo están las cosas
days.objective: Use estar with adjectives to describe feelings and current states, the condition someone or something is in right now.
days.paretoFocus: You say how you feel dozens of times a day, and Spanish marks that meaning with a completely different verb from the one it uses for identity, so the choice is unavoidable from the first conversation.
drills: Say estoy bien and estoy cansado/cansada.
Say a sentence describing a current state with está.
Ask a partner how they are using estar.

items: Give three adjectives commonly used with estar for feelings.
Explain why cansado agrees in gender.
Say a sentence with está abierto/a.

activities.title: Estar + estado
activities.intro: Estar combines with an adjective to report a state: how someone feels, or how something stands at this moment, rather than what defines it. Compare es alegre, cheerfulness as part of who she is, with está alegre, cheerful today. The adjective still agrees in gender and number with its subject, so a group of women says estamos cansadas.

items.note: a fixed, very common reply.
cansado agrees with a masculine subject.
cansada, feminine agreement.
abierta describes the state the shop is in right now.
cerrado, masculine, matches banco.

activities.title: Estados con estar
activities.intro: Match each feeling or state to the right form of estar.

questions.prompt: Which adjective describes a state you are in, not an identity?
questions.explanation: cansado describes the state someone is in, the kind of meaning estar is for; español, estudiante and profesor describe identity.

questions.prompt: What is the feminine form of 'cansado'?
questions.explanation: -o adjectives change to -a for feminine agreement, the same pattern from the adjective lessons.

questions.prompt: Complete: La tienda está ___. (open)
questions.explanation: abierta agrees with the feminine noun tienda and describes the state the shop is in.

questions.prompt: Complete: to speak with a group of friends in Spain, you use ___.
questions.explanation: vosotros is the informal plural in the peninsular system, taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'The bank is closed.'
questions.explanation: cerrado agrees with the masculine banco.

activities.title: ¿Cómo estás?
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people ask how each other feels and describe whether places are open or closed.

days.title: Ser o estar: la primera distinción clara
days.objective: Choose between ser and estar by asking whether the sentence defines something or states what condition it is in, rather than by guessing how long it lasts.
days.paretoFocus: This is the question English speakers ask most, and the rule most of them are taught first, permanent against temporary, is the one that fails. Learning definition against state now prevents years of guessing.
drills: Sort five adjectives by whether they normally pair with ser or estar.
Say one sentence with ser and one with estar about the same person.
Explain the ser/estar difference in your own words.

items: Say three sentences about a friend with ser, defining who they are.
Say three sentences about the same friend with estar, giving their condition today.
Explain in one sentence why está muerto shows that permanent against temporary is the wrong rule.

activities.title: Ser vs estar
activities.intro: Ser states what something IS: identity, origin, profession, what a thing is made of. Estar states what STATE it is in: where it is, how it feels, how it turned out. Be careful with the rule you may have heard, that ser is permanent and estar is temporary. It breaks at once, because esta muerto uses estar and nothing is more permanent than that. Ask what the sentence is DOING, not how long it lasts.

items.en: He is nice. (that is what he is like)
items.note: ser: this defines him.

items.en: He is angry. (that is the state he is in)
items.note: estar: a state he is in, not a definition of him.
ser + de: origin is part of who he is.
estar + en: location is a state, whether it lasts a day or a lifetime.
estar, and permanent. This is why the permanent-versus-temporary rule fails and definition-versus-state does not.

activities.title: Ser o estar
activities.intro: Practice choosing ser or estar for identity versus state.

questions.prompt: Which verb describes a person's origin?
questions.explanation: ser + de states where someone is from, part of what defines them.

questions.prompt: Which sentence states a condition rather than defining the person?
questions.explanation: Está enfadado gives his current condition. Es alto, es de Sevilla and es estudiante all define who he is. Neither choice is about how long it lasts.

questions.prompt: Complete: Ella ___ simpática. (is, an inherent trait)
questions.explanation: ser describes an inherent trait like being nice.

questions.prompt: Complete with the pronoun for a group that excludes the speaker: ___ están en Madrid. (they)
questions.explanation: ellos/ellas refers to a group excluding speaker and listener, taught earlier.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'He is angry.'
questions.explanation: estar marks the state he is in rather than what defines him, and the subject pronoun is optional but allowed for contrast.

activities.title: ¿Cómo es? ¿Cómo está?
activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people describe a friend's lasting traits with ser and his current mood and location with estar.

lines.hr: No, es de Sevilla, pero está en Madrid.
lines.en: No, he's from Sevilla, but he's in Madrid.

lines.speaker: Partner
lines.en: And you? What are you like?

days.title: Hay: decir qué existe
days.objective: Use the invariable form hay to say what exists or is available, with a singular or plural noun.
days.paretoFocus: Hay is how you point out what's around you, in a room, a town or a shop, and it never changes form no matter what follows it.
drills: Say hay + a singular noun and hay + a plural noun.
Say a negative sentence with no hay.
Ask whether something exists nearby using hay.

items: Explain why hay never changes form.
Give a sentence with hay and a plural noun.
Give a negative sentence with hay.

activities.title: Hay
activities.intro: Hay comes from the verb haber and is used only in this one invariable form to say something exists; it works the same with a singular or a plural noun, and un/una or a number can follow it.

items.note: hay + un + singular noun.
hay does not change even with a plural noun.
no before hay for a negative.

items.en: Is there a pharmacy around here?
items.note: hay works in questions the same way.
hay stays the same regardless of number.

activities.title: Hay
activities.intro: Insert hay into short sentences naming things that exist nearby.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct form of hay for a plural noun?
questions.explanation: hay is invariable; it never changes for plural.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is negative?
questions.explanation: no before hay makes the sentence negative.

questions.prompt: Complete: ___ un banco cerca. (there is)
questions.explanation: hay states that something exists.

questions.prompt: Complete: Nosotros ___ español. (speak)
questions.explanation: hablamos is the nosotros form of hablar, from the -ar verb pattern.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'There are three chairs.'
questions.explanation: hay stays the same before both singular and plural nouns.

activities.intro: Play 'Me'. Two people ask whether a pharmacy, a bank, chairs and milk exist nearby.

days.title: Hay o está: información nueva frente a información conocida
days.objective: Choose between hay and está based on whether the noun is new, indefinite information or something specific and already known.
days.paretoFocus: This is the second half of the hay puzzle: hay introduces something for the first time, está points to something both speakers already have in mind, and mixing them up is a very common beginner error.
drills: Say a question with hay about something indefinite.
Say a question with está about something definite.
Explain the hay/está rule in your own words.

items: State the rule for when to use hay.
State the rule for when to use está.
Give a pair of questions, one with hay and one with está, about the same kind of place.

activities.title: Hay vs está
activities.intro: Hay introduces new or indefinite information, usually with un/una or a number, and asks or states whether something exists. Está points to something specific that both speakers already know about, usually with el/la, and says where it is.

items.en: Is there a cash machine around here?
items.note: indefinite, new information: hay.
the farmacia is now known: está + el/la.

items.hr: Hay un banco en la plaza.
items.en: There's a bank in the square.
items.note: introducing the bank for the first time.

items.hr: El banco está en la plaza.
items.en: The bank is in the square.
items.note: a specific, already-known bank.
asking about indefinite availability.

activities.title: Hay o está
activities.intro: Practice choosing hay for new information and está for something already known.

questions.prompt: Which sentence introduces new information?
options: El banco está en la plaza.
Hay un banco en la plaza.
questions.answer: Hay un banco en la plaza.
questions.explanation: hay introduces something for the first time, here an indefinite bank.

questions.prompt: Which sentence refers to something already known?
questions.explanation: está with la farmacia points to a specific, already-known pharmacy.

questions.explanation: vives is the tú form of vivir, from the -ir verb pattern taught a few lessons ago.

questions.prompt: Build the Spanish for: 'Where is the pharmacy?'
questions.explanation: está + la + noun asks about a specific, already-known place.

days.title: Un, una: los artículos indeterminados
days.objective: Use un/una/unos/unas correctly and know when Spanish drops the indefinite article entirely.
days.paretoFocus: English speakers over-use 'a/an' in Spanish; knowing when to drop it fixes one of the most frequent beginner errors.
drills: Write 5 sentences with 'tengo un/una ___'.
List 3 professions and say them with and without an adjective.
Say aloud 3 things there are in your kitchen using 'hay'.

items: Say your profession without an article.
Say there is a book on the table.
Say you have a car.

activities.title: Un, una, unos, unas
activities.intro: Un/una/unos/unas work like 'a/an/some' in English, but Spanish drops them completely after ser with an unmodified profession, nationality or religion.

items.hr: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
items.en: I have a brother and a sister.

items.hr: Hay unos libros en la mesa.
items.en: There are some books on the table.
items.note: unos/unas = 'some', often left untranslated in English
no article before a bare profession

items.en: I am a very patient teacher.
items.note: the article returns once an adjective is added
no article needed for general possession with tener

activities.title: Un, una y su ausencia
activities.intro: Practise when to use the indefinite article and when to drop it.

questions.prompt: ¿Qué frase es correcta?
